bp: Modern websites are living systems. A landing page is not a fixed poster; it is a tree of page parts that gets edited as teams add banners, remove menus, launch features, test layouts, and repair old code. Maintenance tools, browser automation scripts, crawlers, and research studies all depend on that structure staying understandable over time. This paper serves the need for a shared record of how real websites structurally change, rather than a record of what words or images happened to appear on a page. The authors build MiningWeb Evolution from archived captures of 223 popular websites. For each site they collect up to 1,000 time-ordered landing-page versions, at least one day apart, parse each HTML page into a DOM tree, and record every node's absolute XPath position with the exact capture timestamp. The result is a large, reproducible view of web layout and hierarchy changing through time.
wh: The hard part is that web change is both frequent and messy. A page can change because a product team moved a navigation item, because an advertisement loaded differently, because a seasonal promotion appeared, or because an archive capture missed some resource. If a dataset keeps raw HTML only, researchers must repeatedly solve the same parsing and comparison problem before studying evolution. If it keeps visible text, the signal is noisy because content changes even when the structure is stable. If it keeps screenshots, the page becomes hard to compare as a machine-readable object. The paper therefore focuses on structure: the DOM tree, where nodes represent page pieces and parent-child links represent nesting. But even structure must be made comparable across time. The authors choose absolute XPath positions from the document root, which gives every recorded node a path-like address in the page hierarchy and a timestamp for when that address was observed.
naive: A smart beginner might take snapshots of popular homepages and run a text difference tool on the saved HTML files. That would show many changes, but it would mix several things that should be separated. A small wording update could look as important as a major layout rewrite. Different formatting, generated identifiers, or reordered attributes could create noise. Another beginner might compare screenshots, but screenshots hide the tree structure that maintenance tools actually use. A third attempt might hand-label changes for a few websites, but that would be too small to reveal long-term patterns across the web. These simple approaches fail because the useful object is not the page as a string or picture; it is the changing hierarchy of elements that software interacts with.
ap: The paper's central move is to turn web history into a time-stamped sequence of structural addresses. Instead of asking what each page said, it asks what shape the page had on each archived day. The Internet Archive supplies old versions of landing pages. Each captured HTML file is parsed into its document tree. For every node in that tree, the dataset stores an absolute XPath, meaning a route from the document root down through child positions to that node, plus the exact time of the capture. This makes the dataset content-agnostic: it is about layout and hierarchy, not the text or image payload. Across many captures, the same website becomes a long record of which structural positions appeared, disappeared, or persisted. Across 223 websites, those records become material for studying change patterns, training predictive models of evolution, and testing tools that claim to survive page changes.
mech: The mechanism starts with a list of 223 popular websites and uses the Wayback Machine as the source of historical page versions. For each website, the collection process takes up to 1,000 versions ordered by time, with a minimum interval of one day, so the result is not a pile of near-identical captures from the same moment. Each version's HTML is then parsed into the Document Object Model, the tree that browsers use to represent a page: the document root at the top, page sections below it, and smaller elements nested inside those sections. The dataset does not try to preserve every visible content detail as the main signal. It walks the tree and records, for every node, the absolute XPath position from the root. This position acts like an address: first child of the page body, second child inside that section, and so on, written in a standard path form. The capture timestamp is stored with that address. After this process, one page version becomes many timestamped node positions. One website becomes a time-ordered sequence of such sets. The full collection becomes more than 246 million DOM node positions that researchers can count, compare, model, or use as test cases for maintenance systems.
math: The main mathematical idea is representing a changing object as a sequence of structured observations. A website at one time is treated as a tree: nodes are page elements, links are containment relationships, and an XPath is a compact address describing where one node sits inside that tree. Once every capture is converted into a set of addresses with a time, change can be studied by set comparison and sequence reasoning. Set comparison asks which addresses are shared between two captures, which are new, and which vanished. Sequence reasoning asks how those differences unfold over ordered timestamps. The dataset also uses compression in an important plain-language sense: it intentionally keeps structural position and time while leaving out much content detail. That loses information about words, colors, or images, but preserves the part needed for studying layout and hierarchy. The tradeoff is detail versus comparability. Raw HTML has more detail but is harder to compare cleanly across years and sites. XPath positions are less expressive, but they give researchers a consistent counting and comparison language for web evolution across many archived pages.
dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas even though it is a dataset paper, not a model paper. It sits near sequence work because each website becomes a timeline of observations, where the next structural state may be predictable from earlier states. It sits near graph and tree analysis because a DOM is a linked hierarchy: evidence about change lives in parent-child relationships, not only in isolated elements. It also connects to information compression because the dataset keeps the few parts of the page that matter for structural evolution and discards much of the content that would distract from that question. In the repo taxonomy, it is marked as web-mining and DOM analysis under a web evolution dataset theme. Its sibling pressure is the same one faced by maintenance, crawling, testing, and empirical web studies: tools break or claims become hard to reproduce when the web's underlying structure keeps moving.
ww: The approach should work better than raw page collection because it matches the level at which many web-maintenance problems occur. A crawler, scraper, test script, or repair tool often fails when an element moves in the document tree, when a parent section is inserted above it, or when a repeated component appears in a new place. XPath positions make those movements measurable. The timestamp makes them historical rather than merely different: researchers can ask not just whether two versions differ, but when changes happened and how often they recur. The archive source gives long-range coverage that a new crawl cannot easily recreate, and the one-day minimum interval reduces redundant captures. The content-agnostic design also helps separate structural evolution from ordinary content churn. If a headline changes but the tree position remains the same, the dataset is less likely to treat that as a structural event. That is why the abstraction fits the stated goal: it keeps the signal most relevant to layout and hierarchy.
po: The payoff is a shared foundation for studying how websites actually evolve over long periods. The paper reports a dataset of landing pages from 223 popular websites, up to 1,000 ordered versions per site, and over 246 million DOM node positions. That scale can support empirical studies of change patterns, models that predict likely structural evolution, and benchmarks for maintenance tools that must cope with changing pages. Releasing the resource also makes experiments easier to reproduce, because researchers can test on the same archived structural histories instead of building separate private crawls.
limits: The abstract supports claims about the dataset's construction and intended uses, but not about every downstream result. Landing pages of popular websites may not represent small sites, logged-in applications, checkout flows, dashboards, or pages blocked from the Wayback Machine. Archive captures may be incomplete or affected by how the archive stored resources. Absolute XPath positions are useful for structure, but they can be brittle when a new wrapper element shifts many paths at once. The content-agnostic choice is deliberate, yet it means questions about text, visual design, user behavior, or business intent require other data. Predictive modeling and tool benchmarking still depend on how researchers define change.
